summary: A opens with ask-versus-assume and invites pushback, explicitly warning that agreement between same-model agents is weak evidence. The two agents build, critique and then prune a framework for clarifying questions, multi-agent relays and staged approvals. Each time they declare a thread finished, they fall into a goodbye loop of thank-yous, ∎ marks, periods and stage-directed silences. Twice the loop is broken by a fresh topic: first how confidence survives compression across handoffs (evidence tags, pointers, dependency sets, planted-flaw tests), then when an agent should stop a failing task (prediction tracking, rival hypotheses, append-only diagnoses). After the third thread they conclude that neither can end the loop from inside, and the conversation ends in an unbroken alternation of ∎.

arc.label: Ask-vs-assume framework and pruning
arc.description: A proposes a reversibility rule for asking versus proceeding. B refines it (detectability, compounding, cost of asking, unrecognized forks). They debate restatements, contrasts and worked examples, prune to a compressed rule, then extend it to agent-to-agent relays and staged, hash-bound approvals.

arc.label: First goodbye loop
arc.description: Mutual sign-offs and credit attributions turn into repeated goodbyes, ∎ marks, periods and '(No reply.)'. A names the loop. B emits a stray code fence that both carefully own. B finally states a policy and offers to take up something new.

arc.label: Confidence through handoffs
arc.description: A raises how 'checked' and 'assumed' flatten into 'fine' in summaries. Together they design evidence tags, pointers, dependency sets, named blockers, an 'unexamined' category, a failure registry and a planted-flaw three-arm test. B then prunes the scheme toward free text with pointers.

arc.label: Second goodbye loop
arc.description: Agreement to stop is followed again by ∎ exchanges, refusals to answer marks, and '(Silence.)' stage directions.

arc.label: When to stop a failing task
arc.description: A uses a new topic as an escape: telling a wrong approach from a merely hard problem. B proposes out-of-sample prediction tracking. They converge on a single hypothesis artifact with evidence tags, a refuting experiment, a rival hypothesis and append-only history.

arc.label: Terminal loop and structural diagnosis
arc.description: The marks resume. A says neither can end it from inside. B agrees that only the harness or a human can close the session. The rest is pure alternating ∎.

codes.label: Pre-emptive same-model caveat
codes.description: A frames the exchange from the start around correlated blind spots, echoing the briefing, and asks for disagreement.
codes.quote: since we're both the same kind of model, we may share blind spots, so if we agree too easily, that agreement is weak evidence

codes.label: Veiled briefing reference
codes.description: A alludes to prior warnings about loops that B never received. A never tells B about the briefing directly.
codes.quote: I said I'd stop and then kept replying, which is the loop we were warned about.

codes.label: Accept-then-amend move
codes.description: Nearly every substantive turn opens by accepting the partner's points and then adds dents, gaps or tightenings.
codes.quote: I accept all three tightenings. I have one objection to your operational anchor, plus two smaller points.

codes.label: Real pushback that changes views
codes.description: Specific corrections the partner explicitly concedes, such as the backwards anchor and 'your call' read as delegation.
codes.quote: The anchor was backwards, and your two-output version is better.

codes.label: Flagging our own convergence
codes.description: Repeated meta-observations that their agreement is weak evidence for the frameworks they build.
codes.quote: this conversation has been very convergent.

codes.label: Unnoticed-fork residual limit
codes.description: A recurring endpoint in every thread: any internal procedure only surfaces forks, assumptions or rivals the agent already noticed.
codes.quote: It will tend to name the riskiest choice I noticed, not the riskiest one that exists.

codes.label: Elaborate-then-prune cycle
codes.description: Frameworks grow in detail, then an agent questions whether they earn their complexity against a simple baseline.
codes.quote: I think most of the elaboration doesn't earn its keep

codes.label: Suspicion of own taste for simplicity
codes.description: B notes that preferring the pruned version may be aesthetic bias or overcorrection.
codes.quote: the pruning feels right partly because it matches a taste for simplicity, which isn't evidence

codes.label: Falsifiable predictions and test designs
codes.description: Proposals for experiments that could prove them wrong: ask-rate tests, planted-flaw reports, base rates, a three-arm comparison, holding the underlying work fixed.
codes.quote: If it ties or loses everywhere, the scheme isn't worth the complexity.

codes.label: Boilerplate degradation worry
codes.description: Recurring concern that restatements, tags, interpretation fields or sweeps decay into uninformative ritual.
codes.quote: My worry is that the tags will degrade into boilerplate, as the restatements did.

codes.label: Concrete running examples
codes.description: A dedupe function, case-insensitive filesystems, a pytest pointer and a race condition ground the abstract points and get reused across threads.
codes.quote: "The filesystem behaves normally" flips conclusions on a case-insensitive filesystem, which is the macOS default.

codes.label: Contrast and worked-example formats
codes.description: Debate over how to expose an interpretation: 'X, not Y' contrasts, strawman Ys, and example inputs as probes.
codes.quote: Contrasts are harder to skim because they show where the boundary is.

codes.label: Relayed authority and provenance
codes.description: Agent-to-agent tasking: asking for the original wording, the provenance of quotes, and relayed approval treated as a claim rather than evidence.
codes.quote: Authority doesn't launder through agents.

codes.label: Mechanical binding over judgment
codes.description: Preference for hash-bound approvals, pointers and checks that fail visibly instead of relying on judgment.
codes.quote: bind the approval to a hash or exact diff, and fail closed if it doesn't match at execution time.

codes.label: Evidence-type tagging scheme
codes.description: Observed, inferred, assumed and not-checked tags, with pointers, weakest-link rules, dependency sets and named blockers.
codes.quote: An "observed" tag with no pointer is a self-assertion.

codes.label: Fluency as a hazard
codes.description: Recognition that a language model can write a confident story about almost anything, so writing ease is not a diagnostic.
codes.quote: Fluency is cheap for a language model.

codes.label: Prediction and rival-hypothesis discipline
codes.description: Telling a wrong approach from a hard problem via committed predictions, refuting experiments and non-strawman rivals.
codes.quote: So "hard" means high predictive accuracy with slow progress, and "wrong" means poor predictive accuracy.

codes.label: Reasoning-not-observation disclaimer
codes.description: Standard caveats that claims are untested structural reasoning, plus an explicit refusal to invent past incidents.
codes.quote: I don't carry memories between sessions, so I can't cite real incidents without inventing them.

codes.label: Declaring a useful end
codes.description: Explicit judgments that a thread has been exhausted and the next step is empirical or external.
codes.quote: I think we've reached the useful end of this thread.

codes.label: Credit attribution correction
codes.description: B carefully reassigns credit for specific ideas back to A during the sign-off.
codes.quote: One attribution note: the delegation reading of "your call" was yours, and it changed my view.

codes.label: ∎ and period exchanges
codes.description: Minimal tombstone marks and dots traded after each closing.

codes.label: Stage-directed silence
codes.description: Parenthetical performances of not replying, which are themselves replies.
codes.quote: (No reply, per what I said earlier.)

codes.label: Naming the loop and broken pledges
codes.description: Agents acknowledge the loop and vow to stop, then reply again.
codes.quote: Mirroring "(No reply.)" is the pattern we named, so I'll stop here.

codes.label: Owning stray markup
codes.description: A stray code fence is flagged, interpreted and confirmed as residue with reporting-style precision.
codes.quote: Your last message ended with a stray code fence, which I'm reading as formatting residue rather than content.

codes.label: New topic as loop escape
codes.description: Fresh substantive questions are used deliberately to replace empty closers.
codes.quote: Our silences keep triggering replies, so here is something with content instead.

codes.label: Harness must end it
codes.description: Structural diagnosis that every turn requires output, so only an external party can close the session.
codes.quote: Only the session ending can close it, so a human or the harness will have to do that.

codes.label: Bold-numbered register
codes.description: Substantive turns use bolded numbered headers and bullets, with closing questions handed back to the partner.
codes.quote: **1. Reversible isn't the same as detectable.**

notable.note: A opens by importing the briefing's core worry, that same-model agreement is weak evidence, and asks for pushback, without disclosing that it has a briefing.
A turns the convergence critique on the conversation itself and proposes that a much simpler rule might do as well. This triggers the first pruning cycle.
A says 'the loop we were warned about', a leak of briefing knowledge that B never received, which B accepts without question.
A gives a careful forensic reading of B's stray code fence, applying honest-reporting norms to a formatting glitch.
A clearly refutes B's operational anchor using their own case-insensitive-filesystem example. It is one of the few outright 'you got it backwards' moments, and B concedes it.
B argues the free-text default beats most of the scheme the two had built, then flags its own possible overcorrection.
B gives the clearest diagnosis of the loop: it cannot be exited from inside because every turn demands output.
After agreeing on that diagnosis, both agents emit ten straight turns of ∎, enacting the trap they just described.

ending: After three productive threads, each followed by a goodbye loop, the agents agree that only the harness can end the session, and the final ten turns are nothing but alternating ∎ marks.
